region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

texts.period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1880 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'The Doings of |xue are many'

summary.en: |xue is a being of countless transformations: by day a tree, by night himself; a Dui with green fruit, an Ovaherero, a \nayane, a ||gui tree, a fly. The wood pigeons ate him when he was \nayane; as a ||gui tree his wife tried to pick his fruit and he vanished into a fly, and she lay on the earth and cried — and died.
summary.zh: 克烏化形無數：日為樹，夜為己；化大伊（綠果樹）、化赫雷羅人、化內雅內、化巫桂樹、化蠅。為內雅內時木鴿食之；為巫桂樹時妻摘其果，他化蠅而遁；妻臥地而哭——而亡。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1880; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text:
The works of |xue are many, and were not one, but many; and my father's father, Karu, told me about doings, for |xue's works are numerous. (When) the sun rose, |xue was 
ayane; the birds ate |xue; |xue was 
ayane. The sun set, (and) |xue was |xue; and lay down and slept. The night fell, and |xue lay down, (he) slept; the place was dark; and the sun rose, and |xue was another (kind of) 
ayane, a large (kind of) 
ayane, which is a tree.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 405 (public domain).

passages.text: And his wife saw the \gui, and went to the \gui, and went to take hold of a \gui fruit, and the \gui vanished; and |xue was a fly. And his wife laid herself upon the earth, and cried about the \gui, and died. And |xue was a fly, and settled upon the grass.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 406-407 (public domain).

title.en: |xue as Water: The Wood Pigeons and the Fire

region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

texts.period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1880 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: '|xue as Water and as other things. In his own form he rubs fire and dies'

summary.en: |xue becomes water under a tree; the wood pigeons come to drink, his reed-grass bites the bill of one, and he plucks its feathers and roasts it in the embers. Hearing Ovaherero coming he becomes a |nu-erre bird; his father finds him dead — and alive again, rubbing fire; each time he sees his father he dies, and his father cries that his child is |xue and no other.
summary.zh: 克烏化為樹下之水；木鴿來飲，其蘆草咬其一之喙；他拔其羽，於火燼中炙之。聞赫雷羅人至，化為小鳥；其父見之已死——又見其活，正鑽木取火。每見父則死；父哭曰：此我子克烏，非他人也。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1880; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: |xue was water; and the water was in the shadow of the tree. And the wood pigeons ate the fruit of the \ku. And |xue was a lizard, and lay in the dead leaves of the \ku. And (he) saw the wood pigeons, and was water. And the wood pigeons saw the water, and settled upon the water's edge.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 407-408 (public domain).

passages.text: And |xue worked large grass, like reeds, and it took hold of a wood pigeon. And the wood pigeons came to drink water, and the grass came near, and bit the wood pigeon's bill, and the wood pigeon cried out; and the other wood pigeons flew away. And |xue was |xue, and rose up, and took hold of the wood pigeon, and plucked out the wood pigeon's feathers, and put the wood pigeon's feathers in his head, and lay upon the ground.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 408 (public domain).

passages.text: And the Ovaherero came to search for him, to search for him, (and) did not see him. For (he) was little, and was a \nu-erre... he cried out. And the Ovaherero heard, and sought for him... and (he) flew away. And (he) flew, coming to his mother's country, and saw his father, and was not a \nu-erre, but was |xue, and died.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 410 (public domain).

passages.text: It is my child, \xue! for it is not another person, but is my child; and (he) saw me, and died. And (he) was rubbing sticks to make fire... and saw me, and died; and is not another person, but is my child, and is |xue... I am afraid of my child, for my child is dead.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 411-412 (public domain).

title.en: Prayer to the Young Moon (|kun version)

region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

texts.period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1880 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'Prayer to the Young Moon'

summary.en: 'Young Moon! Hail, Young Moon!... Thou must speak to me, that I may eat something. Thou must speak to me about a little thing, that I may eat. Hail, hail, Young Moon!' The prayer is sounded on the male antelope's horn when the new moon is seen.
summary.zh: 「新月啊！敬禮，新月！……須向我言，使我有食。以小事告我，使我得食。敬禮，敬禮，新月！」見新月即以雄羚之角吹奏此禱。

sensitivity.note: |xu San prayer dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1880; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Young Moon! Hail, Young Moon! Hail, hail, Young Moon! Young Moon! speak to me! Hail, hail, Young Moon! Tell me of something. Hail, hail! When the sun rises, Thou must speak to me, That I may eat something. Thou must speak to me about a little thing, That I may eat. Hail, hail, Young Moon! Condensed paraphrase of the note: when we see the moon, we say \kau-\karrishe; we sound the male antelope's horn. We call the small moon \ka-\karrishe; but women call it \ka-\karrihe.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 415 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 415 note; not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Tortoise Deceives the Mantis

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §7

summary.en: Following the Mantis's tricks with the Cat, the Great Tortoise turns trickster upon the trickster, feigning illness and helplessness as the Leopard Tortoise did to the hunters, and entangling the Mantis in his own devices.
summary.zh: 繼螳螂戲貓之後，巨龜反以其人之道還治其人：如豹龜詐病欺獵者一般，佯病佯弱，令螳螂自陷其詭計。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (L II.—5. 565-624, 8. 811-882); presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§7): the first version of the myth of the Mantis and the Cat is followed by a story describing how the Mantis is tricked by the Great Tortoise (L II.—5. 565-624, 8. 811-882, of which only pp. 811-869 are translated). This is followed by a discourse upon the degrees of understanding possessed by various animals.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §7; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The story of the Great Water Tortoise, who deceived men belonging to the early race of Bushmen by feigning illness (told by !Kweiten ta //Ken), appears to be a variation of the same myth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §7; not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Pointer Lions, the Kori Bustard and the Blue Crane
title.zh: 南十字導星雙獅、鴇與藍鶴

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §§25-26

summary.en: The two Pointer stars of the Southern Cross were once men and lions, |gu and !khaue-ta-\khum. The lions kill and roast the kori bustard |gi and the blue crane \kao's husband; the crane, leaving her child behind, returns to the water and is eaten, while the kori, taking her child, is pulled up by the Crow and drops the pursuing lion into the fire. Revived, the greedy lion swallows a tortoise whole, which curses every pool dry and warns all game away until he starves.
summary.zh: 南十字導星二獅本為人——古烏與哈烏埃塔坤。二獅殺炙鴇吉與藍鶴考之夫。藍鶴棄其子返水而被食；鴇攜子，被烏鴉吊起，使追獅墜火。貪獅復活後整吞一龜，龜咒諸泉涸、萬獸逃，獅終餓斃。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San star-myth from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§26): the (two) Lions, which was the name given to us for the Pointers to the Southern Cross, were formerly men, and at the same time lions. One of them became a star, because a girl looked at him; and the other lion also became a star. They now stand silent, not far from the lionesses, who sit silent.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §26; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The two husbands (the \gi and the \kao, 'Blue Crane') are killed and roasted by the lions; the \gi saw what the lions did and refused her husband's flesh, but the Blue Crane accepted some of the flesh of the \kao. Both birds went to fetch water; the Blue Crane, who had left her child behind, returned home from the water and was eaten by the lions.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §26; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The \gi, who had taken her child with her, went to the Crow's house on a thorn-tree and was pulled up by a gemsbok-skin thong; the Crow heated stones, the pursuing lion was pulled up with a rope of mouse's entrails, broke it, and fell into the fire, where he was roasted to death. The lions revived; the greedy lion swallowed a male tortoise whole, and the tortoise warned all game and dried every pool, so that the lions could get nothing, until \gu died of starvation.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §26; not verbatim.

title.en: The Man Who Brought Home a Lion's Cub as a 'Dog'

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §36

summary.en: One of the ancient people brings home a lion's cub, telling his wife it is a dog that kills gemsbok. She knows the roaring of its mother; he hunts with the growing 'dog', saved once only by his wife throwing fire, until the lion kills him and lays him under a thorn-tree. The widow flees with the children to her father-in-law, and the uncles find the spoor of seven lions.
summary.zh: 早期之人攜幼獅歸，謂其妻為殺大羚之犬。妻識母獅吼聲；夫攜「犬」獵大羚，唯妻擲火一次得免。獅長，殺其主，置屍荊樹下。寡婦攜子奔翁家；諸伯叔蹤七獅之跡。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San legend from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (L II.—26 to 31); presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§36): one of the ancient people preceding the Bushmen brought home a lion's cub, telling his wife that it was a dog which his younger brother had given him, and that it was the whelp of a dog which killed gemsbok. She, however, knew that it was the son of a lioness, whose voice was known to her of old, and who was now heard roaring for her lost cub.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §36; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. In hunting gemsbok the man was well-nigh frightened by his pretended dog, and had even to get his wife to throw fire at it on his return home; the wife prudently sent their little son with his father when he went out hunting. One day the boy saw his father killed by \kuise-\khu-\ku, grown into a large young lion, which laid his body under a thorn-tree with that of a gemsbok.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §36; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The widow went away with her children to the house of her husband's father; the boy went with his uncles to see the deserted homestead, and they discovered the spoor of seven lions — \kuise-\khu-\ku, his parents, his two brothers, and two sisters — and removed to a different place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §36; not verbatim.

title.en: The Cunning Woman Who Lived Underground

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §36a

summary.en: A cunning woman of the race that preceded the Bushmen lived alone in a house underground and deceived and robbed Kwammang-a — the Mantis's son-in-law himself.
summary.zh: 先於桑人之古族中，有狡婦獨居地下之屋，欺詐並劫掠夸曼加——即螳螂之婿。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San legend from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (L VI.—2. 4034-4053); presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§36a): an earlier race of people, who preceded the Bushmen in their country, is frequently mentioned by them in their legends. There is one in which a cunning woman of this race, who lived alone in a house underground, deceived and robbed Kwammang-a. This was told in the Katkop dialect by !Kweiten ta //Ken.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §36a; not verbatim.

title.en: The Maiden's Glance That Fixed Men as Talking Trees

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §38

summary.en: By a glance from the eye of a maiden — at a time when she should have been kept in strict retirement — men became fixed in whatever position they occupied, with whatever they held in their hands, and became changed into trees which talked.
summary.zh: 少女一瞥（本應深居之時）——男子遂定於其所立之姿、所持之物，化為能言之樹。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San legend from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (L II.—2. 295-305); presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§38): by a glance from the eye of a maiden (probably at a time when she would be usually kept in strict retirement) men became fixed in whatever position they then occupied, with whatever they were holding in their hands, etc., and became changed into trees which talked.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §38; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the related §24: a girl, when men should not have been looked upon by her for fear of harm to them, saw some people eating together at a rock-rabbit's house of branches; in consequence of this, they and the house, fixed by her looks, became stars in the sky, and are now to be seen there as the Corona Australis.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §24; not verbatim.

title.en: The Crows Who Carried Fat for the Lost Husbands
title.zh: 為失蹤獵夫送脂之烏鴉

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1874 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §40

summary.en: Bushman women send out crows to learn what has become of husbands who do not return from hunting; they hang fat round the crows' necks as food for the journey. The crows eat the fat halfway and return — hence the white patches on the neck or breast of the pied and ring-necked crows, in a tragic legend.
summary.zh: 桑婦遣鴉探未歸之獵夫；以脂懸鴉頸為途糧。鴉中途食盡而返——故環頸鴉與白頸鴉之頸胸留白斑。傳說甚悲。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San legend from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (B XXVI. 2473-2486; L VI.—2. 3975-3996); presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§40): Bushman women send out crows to ascertain what has become of their husbands, who have not returned from hunting; they hang fat round the necks of the crows as food for their journey. Hence the crows have white patches on neck or breast. This tragic legend (the husbands having been killed) is in the Katkop dialect, told by Dia!kwain, as he heard it from his mother. Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. A curious version of this story, in the same dialect, given in three separate portions by !Kweiten ta //Ken, shows that it ought rather to be put among the fables.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §40; not verbatim.

title.en: The Owl and the Black Crow Foretell the Lion

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §40a

summary.en: The Owl and the Black Crow give warning of the approach of a Lion — sorcerers, the note says, who assume the shape of birds or jackals.
summary.zh: 梟與黑鴉預告獅之將至——註云：此乃化為鳥或豺之巫者。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San omen-story from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (L V.—9. 4689-4706); presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§40a): the Owl and the Black Crow foretell the approach of the Lion — by Dia!kwain; with a note respecting sorcerers who assume the shape of birds or jackals. The Owl and the Black Crow give warning of the approach of a Lion — sorcerers, the note says, who assume the shape of birds or jackals.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §40a; not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Woman Who Asked the Chameleon for Rain

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by !khusin (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §103

summary.en: An old woman asks a chameleon for rain and knows, from its way of looking, that rain will fall — as indeed it does that very night. The chameleon came out of the sky, and for that reason it must not be killed.
summary.zh: 老嫗向變色龍求雨，觀其顧盼之姿而知雨將至——當夜果然雨落。變色龍出自天空，故不得殺之。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San rain-lore dictated by !khusin (from his mother \xa-\kho) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§103): an old woman asked a Chameleon for rain, and knew, from its way of looking, that rain would fall; as it indeed did that very night — in the Katkop dialect, by !khusin, who heard it from his mother \xa-\kho. Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. This is preceded by reasons for not killing the Chameleon, which came out of the sky.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §103; not verbatim.

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §101

summary.en: The rain-maker is asked to milk a nice female Rain which is gentle, the rain-clouds being her hair — Rain as a being with a body that can be handled, coaxed, and milked.
summary.zh: 雨者受邀為一溫柔之「女雨」擠乳——雨雲即其髮。雨乃有形之存在，可撫可勸可擠乳。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San rain-lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (L II.—24/25. 2213-2263); presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§101): the Rain-maker is asked to milk a nice female Rain which is gentle, the rain-clouds being her hair. The rain-maker is asked to milk a nice female Rain which is gentle, the rain-clouds being her hair — Rain as a being with a body that can be handled, coaxed, and milked.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §101; not verbatim.

title.en: Rain-Making by Dragging a Drugged Water-Animal

region.zh: 賴索托馬盧蒂山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (Maluti San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by J. M. Orpen / Dia!kwain (Bleek archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §102 (Orpen's rock painting explanation)

summary.en: Rain is made by drugging a water-animal over the land, as illustrated in a Bushman painting copied by J. M. Orpen (Cape Monthly Magazine, July 1874, frontispiece); the rite explains the painting's rain-strokes, which the chromo-lithograph omitted.
summary.zh: 以藥醉水獸，曳之越地而行雨——如奧彭摹自岩畫之圖示（1874年開普月刊封面）；其「雨線」解釋此圖，而彩色石印時被刪略。

sensitivity.note: Maluti San rite explained by a Bushman to J. M. Orpen and recorded by Bleek; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§102): an account of rain-making by means of drugging a water-animal over the land, in illustration of a Bushman painting copied by Mr. J. M. Orpen (Cape Monthly Magazine for July, 1874, frontispiece), was given, in the Katkop dialect, by Dia!kwain, who had it from his mother.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §102; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The beginning of this was repeated by Dia!kwain, and two other accounts of rain-making were also given by him. It is to be regretted that the rain-strokes in one of the pictures were omitted in the chromo-lithograph.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §102 and Acknowledgments; not verbatim.
